html:
"English territory" is the map's label for the lands of the kings of England in 1279, 1300 and 1400. It has three parts: England with conquered Wales, the English-held part of Ireland, and Gascony in south-west France.

The Norman Conquest of 1066 and the Angevin kings had tied England to large lands in France, but most were lost in 1204. What remained was Gascony, around Bordeaux, rich from the wine trade. Edward I conquered Wales in the 1280s and tried to conquer Scotland. In Ireland the English held the east, around Dublin, after the Anglo-Norman invasion.

The claim of Edward III to the French throne started the Hundred Years' War in 1337. England won great battles and took Calais, but by 1453 it had lost everything in France except Calais, which fell in 1558. The state behind these lands is the chart's England, then Britain.
sum: "English territory" is the map's label for the lands of the kings of England in 1279, 1300 and 1400. It has three parts: England with conquered Wales, the English-held part of Ireland, and Gascony in south-west France.
